Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn The Bucharest Court of Appeal suspended six of 11 government decisions challenged by the opposition Social Democratic Party (PSD), according to Digi24 . Two of the suspended decisions concern milestones that Romania must meet under the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). The court examined six of the 11 challenges on July 30 and suspended all six. The remaining five cases are due to be heard next week, most likely on August 3. The PSD had initially challenged 12 government decisions, but acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan withdrew the decision concerning the National Strategy for Biodiversity Conservation 2026-2030 two days before the court hearing. The biodiversity strategy is also an RRF milestone. The two suspended decisions linked directly to RRF milestones concern the reorganisation of the Ministry of Agriculture and the granting of housing and transitional benefits to adults with severe, serious or moderate disabilities leaving public residential centres. Romania must complete the relevant RRF milestones by the end of August to secure the associated EU funding. The court decisions therefore add uncertainty to the government’s efforts to meet the deadlines. The PSD’s legal challenge is part of a broader confrontation between the party and the minority government led by Bolojan, amid a continuing political deadlock. The Social Democrats have sought to challenge government decisions adopted during the interim period, arguing that the executive has exceeded its legal authority. PSD president Sorin Grindeanu recently said that no settlement of the political crisis could be reached before August 15, while suggesting that the situation could improve after that date without providing further details. The government has previously warned that court action against decisions implementing RRF commitments could put EU funding at risk. Bolojan said the government had withdrawn the biodiversity decision and sent it to Parliament as a bill to avoid the possibility of its suspension pending a final court ruling. The five remaining cases are expected to be heard next week, while Romania continues to face an end-August deadline for completing the RRF milestones. iulian@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Gov.ro) Read next 29 July 2026 Politics Romania’s SocDem opposition challenges government decisions on PNRR milestones Normal Politics Romania’s Social Democrats seek to hinder government activity through court actions 31 July 2026 Iulian Ernst Like this article? Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images US military US says Iranian tankers ‘destroyed’ after missile attacks on American warship Tit-for-tat violence surges again in region, with tankers struck by the US in the Gulf of Oman, and reprisal attacks by Iran on a US base in Jordan Shrai Popat in Washington Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.04 EDT First published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 16.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US military on Tuesday said it “destroyed” multiple Iranian tankers, after Iran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles, as violence once again surged across the region, pushing the price of oil close to $100 a barrel. American forces struck the tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg Island, US central command (Centcom) said in a statement, adding that American forces “directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck”. Centom said the strikes came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. “The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had struck a US military base in Jordan with in retaliation. Air-defence systems destroyed 18 ⁠of the ⁠20 ​ballistic missiles originating ⁠from Iranian territory, Jordan’s state ⁠news ​agency ‌reported, citing the ‌armed forces, adding that two missiles fell in unpopulated areas ‌and there were no casualties. The Revolutionary Guards Navy also warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for the US attacks. After a month of relative calm in August, Iran and the US have resumed exchanges of fire, sending ‌global oil prices back up to levels last seen in July. Oil prices climbed on Wednesday to near $100 a barrel in early Asia trading. On Tuesday, Yemen’s Iran-backed Hothis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia , wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war. Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south. Remarking on the latest strikes by Iran, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said the US would not let Iran’s attacks to go unanswered. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers. And I think you’ll see that again today,” Rubio said on Tuesday, during a trip to Colombia. The strikes followed an earlier dispute over an American underwater drone in the strait of Hormuz, which the IRGC claimed to have seized as part of a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn”, according to Iranian state TV. In a statement, the IRGC said images of the vessel would be released shortly. In a statement, US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a United States Centcom spokesperson, said the submersible was “defective” and an older model “that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”. Operations in the area continue, he said. Iran has maintained a blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of the global oil and gas shipments, since the outbreak of the war more than six months ago, while the US has imposed its own blockade of Iranian ports. In Paris, South Korean president Lee Jae Myung and French president Emmanuel Macron discussed cooperation on security and freedom of navigation in the strait of Hormuz. South Korea’s defence ministry said it had sent an inspection team to the United Arab Emirates to assess security conditions in the region, but stressed that the mission was intended to gather information and did not presuppose a troop deployment. A South Korean official said Iran had expressed interest and sought explanations through diplomatic channels after media reports about a possible South Korean role in Hormuz security efforts. South Korea’s presidential office ⁠separately said reports that the US had set a deadline for Seoul to send assets ​to Hormuz were untrue. Seoul said last week ​it was reviewing various options, including military ​measures, to contribute to freedom of navigation in Hormuz, but denied reports that the US had set a deadline for Seoul to dispatch assets ​to the strait. Trump has struggled to end the unpopular war, which has claimed the lives of 18 US service members. Iranian authorities have previously put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures that outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated. Russia: Huge flames and smoke rise over St Petersburg after drone strikes Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 18/10/2026 - 16:45 GMT+2 Huge plumes of black smoke billowed over St Petersburg, Russia’s second-largest city, on Sunday, 18 October, as a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack sparked fires at industrial and logistics facilities. Russian officials said 126 drones had been intercepted in the surrounding region. … More Footage shared on social media showed a major blaze at a warehouse operated by Ozon , Russia 's second-largest online retailer, which said its logistics centre had been struck. Other images showed thick smoke rising from the area of the St Petersburg Oil Terminal , while an oil refinery and depot were also reportedly hit. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT St Petersburg's governor, Alexander Beglov , confirmed that air-defence systems had been activated after a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on the city overnight, while Leningrad Region governor Alexander Drozdenko initially reported that 126 drones had been shot down over the surrounding region. He later raised that figure to 144 , with some reports putting it at 145 . The assault set the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot alight and struck infrastructure in several districts of the city. Beglov said one person was killed and five others were injured , while operations at Pulkovo Airport were temporarily restricted for safety reasons. The strikes came as President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after briefly suspending them following Donald Trump’s declaration of an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October. Neither side formally confirmed the arrangement, and Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out 76 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure over the following week, including strikes on substations in four regions that left tens of thousands of families without power. The latest exchange underlines the continuing struggle over energy infrastructure , with both sides treating refineries, terminals and power grids as central targets in a war that shows no sign of abating. Blaine Holt told Newsmax on Monday that European leaders are standing in the way of a diplomatic solution to the Russia-Ukraine war, even as President Donald Trump seeks to ease global energy costs through negotiations with Moscow. Appearing on "Rob Schmitt Tonight," Holt blamed NATO and European Union leaders for prolonging the conflict while resisting Trump's efforts to negotiate an end to the fighting. "Here's your big problem. And we're not talking about them yet. It's Europe, NATO, the EU leaders," Holt said. "They're doubling down on something that they don't have the cards to double down on. They haven't offered one diplomatic solution in this war yet." Holt argued that Europe's energy crisis has made continued fighting increasingly costly, saying diesel prices reaching $11 a gallon in Finland and as much as $13 elsewhere in Europe. "President Trump is trying to offer relief and an avenue toward a diplomatic solution," Holt said. He also defended Trump's efforts to discourage attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that further disruptions to fuel supplies could worsen global economic conditions and contribute to food shortages. "And so, Europe has been the impediment here," Holt said. "Zelenskyy is following their lead. I think, foolishly, there's no military answer to this war." Holt questioned whether additional military assistance to Ukraine could produce a decisive outcome against Russia, arguing that Western leaders have failed to present a workable alternative to negotiations.
